title: Birds That Fly Over Arabia: Migration
summary: Why millions of birds migrate over the Arabian Peninsula each year, how big and small birds make the trip, how they find their way, and where they rest.
poll: Protecting wetlands and oases is important for birds that do not even live here.

versions.title: Birds on the Move
versions.text:
Look up in the fall. You may see a flock of birds in a long line. They migrate. They take a long trip each year.

In the north, the cold comes. The bugs die. The birds can not find food. So they fly south to warm lands in Africa. In spring, they fly back north. They lay eggs there. Each season has its trip.

Our land is on the path. Lots of birds fly past each fall and spring. Some stay all winter. Big eagles stay here.

Big birds like storks do not flap much. They ride on warm air from hot land. The sea has no warm air. So they cross where the sea is thin, near Yemen.

Small birds, like swallows, flap all the way. They eat a lot first. Some get twice as fat!

How do they know the way? They use the sun and stars. They feel the pull of the Earth. They look for coasts and hills.

On the long journey, birds must rest. They stop at a wetland or a farm. They eat and drink. Some folks put a ring on a bird's leg. It shows where the bird flies.

On a cool autumn morning, look up at the sky. You may see a flock of birds moving in a long line toward the south. These birds are on a migration, a long journey that they make at the same time every year.

In the far north, in parts of Europe and Asia, winters are freezing. Insects disappear, and birds can no longer find enough food. So they fly south to warmer lands in Africa. When spring returns, they fly back north to build nests and raise their chicks, because summer there brings plenty of food. Each season starts a new journey.

The Arabian Peninsula lies right in the middle of their route. Scientists call a route like this a flyway. Millions of birds pass over Arabia every autumn and every spring, and some stay for the whole winter. Large steppe eagles, for example, spend the cold months in Saudi Arabia.

Big birds such as storks and eagles rarely flap. Instead, they soar on thermals, which are columns of warm air rising from the hot ground. Thermals do not form over the sea, so these birds avoid long sea crossings. Many cross where the water is narrow, between Yemen and Africa.

Small birds, like swallows, flap the whole way. Many travel at night. Before they leave, they eat so much that some become almost twice as heavy.

How do birds find their way? They use the sun and the stars. They can also sense Earth's magnetic pull, like a compass. They follow coasts and mountains, too.

During the journey, birds need a stopover to rest. They land at a wetland, a farm, or a green oasis to eat and drink. Storms and extreme heat can harm them. Scientists put small rings or trackers on some birds' legs to learn where they travel.

versions.title: Birds That Fly Over Arabia: Migration
versions.text:
On a crisp autumn morning, an attentive observer who gazes upward may notice a flock of birds advancing in a long, undulating line toward the south, pressing onward across the sky with evident collective purpose. These birds are participating in a migration, an extraordinary seasonal journey that they repeat with remarkable consistency at approximately the same time every single year, frequently traversing thousands of kilometers of entirely unfamiliar territory throughout the undertaking.

Throughout the northern regions of Europe and Asia, winters arrive bitterly and unforgivingly freezing, and because insects disappear entirely while vegetation becomes dormant across the landscape, birds can no longer locate sufficient nourishment to survive the season, so they relocate southward toward the considerably warmer territories of sub-Saharan Africa. When spring eventually returns to the north, they journey back northward once again in order to construct nests and raise their vulnerable chicks, since the extended northern summer reliably provides abundant food resources along with substantially lengthier daylight hours for foraging.

The Arabian Peninsula occupies a strategically crucial position directly beneath one of these major migratory routes, which ornithologists precisely designate a flyway, and consequently millions upon millions of individual birds traverse Arabian skies during every single autumn and spring season without exception. Some individuals elect to remain throughout the entire winter rather than continuing their journey onward; enormous steppe eagles, for example, routinely spend the colder winter months residing permanently within Saudi Arabia itself.

Large birds such as storks and eagles seldom flap their wings during the course of migration, preferring instead to soar effortlessly upon thermals, which are invisible columns of warm air continuously ascending from the sun-heated ground far below them. Because thermals rarely develop over open water of any kind, these large birds deliberately avoid lengthy sea crossings whenever such a detour proves possible, and enormous numbers of them consequently concentrate at the Bab al-Mandab, a narrow strait separating Yemen from the African continent at its closest point.

Smaller birds, such as swallows, must flap continuously throughout the entire distance of their arduous journey, and many of them travel specifically at night, when the surrounding atmosphere proves considerably cooler and more favorable for sustained, energy-intensive flight. Before departing on their journey, they consume such substantial quantities of available food that certain individuals become almost twice their normal body weight, storing this considerable additional fat reserve as metabolic fuel for the demanding trip that lies ahead of them.

How, then, do these remarkable long-distance travelers successfully navigate across such vast and often featureless distances? They evidently rely upon the position of the sun and the stars for essential orientation, and they can also detect Earth's magnetic field directly through specialized sensory mechanisms, which functions essentially as an internal biological compass, while additionally recognizing prominent coastlines and mountain ranges as reliable visual landmarks positioned along their established route.

Throughout this demanding journey, exhausted birds require periodic stopovers at wetlands, agricultural fields, or vegetated oases scattered along the way, where they can eat, drink, and gradually recover their severely depleted energy reserves before continuing onward. Violent storms and extreme ambient temperatures can seriously endanger migrating birds at any point along their route, so researchers attach lightweight rings or sophisticated electronic trackers to selected individuals' legs in order to determine precisely where these birds travel across multiple continents over the course of a year. Such coordinated scientific efforts ultimately help communities and governments protect the critical habitats that these remarkable long-distance travelers depend upon absolutely for their continued survival as species.

MID.prompt: Compare how big soaring birds and small birds like swallows make their long journey. Use evidence from the article.
checklist: I described how big birds travel.
I described how small birds travel.
I used at least two details from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: Big soaring birds like storks and eagles rarely flap their wings; instead they ride thermals, columns of warm air rising from the hot ground, and they avoid long sea crossings because thermals do not form over water. Small birds such as swallows travel very differently, since they flap the whole way and many fly at night, eating so much beforehand that some become almost twice as heavy. Both kinds of birds are making the same overall journey across the flyway, but big birds save energy by soaring while small birds rely on constant flapping.

HIGH.prompt: Migrating birds face many challenges on their journey over Arabia. Explain two challenges and how birds overcome them, using evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained two challenges birds face.
I explained how birds overcome each challenge.
I used precise evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: One challenge migrating birds face is crossing large bodies of water, since thermals do not form over the sea and large soaring birds depend on those rising columns of warm air to stay aloft; they overcome this by crossing at the narrow strait between Yemen and Africa instead of flying over open ocean. A second challenge is simply finding the way across such a vast, featureless route like the Arabian flyway; birds overcome this by combining several strategies, sensing Earth's magnetic field like a compass, following the sun and stars, and tracking coastlines and mountains below them. Along the way, they also rely on stopovers at wetlands and oases to rest and refuel before continuing their journey.
